articles.title: MLB rookie overlooked by 181 draft picks lands $50.75m deal before debut, then justifies huge gamble with historic World Series feat seven months later
articles.summary: Cooper Pratt, the 22-year-old rookie shortstop for the Milwaukee Brewers, defies odds after being drafted 182nd overall, proving his worth with a remarkable $50.75 million contract and historic feats in the World Series.
articles.body: Cooper Pratt had played only three games at Triple-A or above when the Milwaukee Brewers decided he was worth a contract worth more than $50 million. It was an extraordinary commitment to a player who had not yet faced a major-league pitcher, but the 22-year-old shortstop has given the organisation an answer far sooner than anyone could have expected. By the time the World Series reached its decisive games, the gamble was beginning to look like one of the smartest decisions the Brewers had made.From Mississippi high school standout to sixth-round draft pickCooper Wickham Pratt was born on August 18, 2004, in Hialeah, Florida, before his family moved to Oxford, Mississippi, where he grew up close to the University of Mississippi. He attended Magnolia Heights School in Senatobia, where his ability with both bat and ball made him one of the state's most promising young baseball players.Pratt's senior season in 2023 was particularly impressive. He batted .469, drove in 50 runs and stole 38 bases, while his work on the mound was just as striking: he finished with a 10-0 record and an extraordinary 0.14 earned run average. His performances earned him Mississippi's Gatorade Player of the Year award.Though he had high hopes of being a first-round pick in the 2023 MLB Draft, 181 players were chosen before the Milwaukee Brewers finally selected him in the sixth round. Disappointed by the slide, Pratt was fully prepared to pivot to college and was actually standing in line at Ole Miss to pick up his campus parking pass when the Brewers called with a life-changing offer.They selected Pratt in the sixth round of the 2023 MLB Draft, 182nd overall, and persuaded him to turn professional rather than take up his college commitment. His signing bonus was $1.35 million, a substantial sum for a sixth-round selection and an early indication that Milwaukee saw considerably more in him than his draft position might suggest.Pratt was a right-handed hitter and thrower, standing six feet four inches tall and weighing 210 pounds. The Brewers were investing in a young shortstop with the physical tools to develop into an important part of their future, although there was still considerable work to do before he could establish himself in professional baseball.The progress that convinced Milwaukee to make an extraordinary offerPratt's development through the minor leagues gave the Brewers increasing confidence in their investment. In 2024, his first full minor-league season, he batted .277, hit eight home runs and stole 27 bases across two levels. The combination of offensive production, speed and defensive ability helped him move up the organisation's prospect rankings.His progress continued in 2025 with Double-A Biloxi. Pratt won a Minor League Gold Glove for his defensive work at shortstop, while the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel ranked him as the Brewers' second-best prospect. He entered the following season as a consensus top-100 prospect, with Baseball America placing him 50th and MLB Pipeline ranking him 64th.Milwaukee had already shown a willingness to commit significant money to young players before they reached the major leagues. In December 2023, the organisation signed outfielder Jackson Chourio to an eight-year, $82 million extension when he was only 19 and had played just six games above Double-A. Chourio subsequently reached the majors in 2024 and recorded at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in each of his first two seasons.That experience provided a precedent, but Pratt's situation was an even more unusual test of the organisation's judgement. On April 3, 2026, the Brewers agreed an eight-year, $50.75 million contract extension with him despite the fact that he had not played a single regular-season game in the majors. He had appeared in only three games at Triple-A or above, and MLB.com reported that no player had previously signed an extension with so little experience in the upper minor leagues.The deal was a major commitment to a prospect whose potential Milwaukee believed justified the risk. It also meant the Brewers would not receive any rewards through Major League Baseball's Prospect Promotion Incentive programme, which can provide draft-pick compensation for certain teams that promote and retain highly regarded prospects. The organisation was effectively choosing long-term control of a player it believed could become its everyday shortstop over the possibility of receiving that additional draft benefit.A major-league debut, followed by a season that justified the faithPratt made his MLB debut on June 16, 2026, more than two months after signing the extension. He did not need long to demonstrate why Milwaukee had been prepared to make such an early commitment.Across 74 regular-season games, the rookie batted .281, hit three home runs, drove in 34 runs and stole 19 bases. His on-base plus slugging percentage was .718, and his performances helped him establish himself as the Brewers' everyday shortstop. For a player who had entered the year without a major-league appearance, he had moved quickly from prospect to an important member of the first team.The Brewers finished the regular season with 103 victories, the most in baseball, and went on to win the National League pennant. It was their first appearance in the World Series since 1982, giving Pratt an opportunity to test himself on the biggest stage in the sport during his very first major-league season.He had already given Milwaukee a significant return on its investment, but the postseason would provide a rather different examination. A rookie shortstop could be protected through the regular season while adjusting to the demands of major-league pitching; the World Series offered no such accommodation.Pratt delivers when the Brewers need him mostPratt made his presence felt early in the World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays. On October 24, in Game 2, he produced a go-ahead single in the seventh inning as Milwaukee won 5-4, taking a 2-0 lead in the series. It was the sort of contribution that does not necessarily dominate a box score but can decide a championship game.His influence continued through the remaining games. In Game 3, Pratt was among the Brewers' seven consecutive hits in the fifth inning, a remarkable stretch of offensive production that helped Milwaukee maintain its pressure on Tampa Bay. By Game 4, he was again involved in one of the series' defining moments.At Tropicana Field in St Petersburg on October 27, Pratt hit a solo home run in the 12th inning to put Milwaukee ahead 3-2. The shot was celebrated as a potential game-winning blow, capping off a massive four-hit night for the shortstop. While the Rays would ultimately rally to win Game 4, that home run marked the peak of an incredibly hot stretch where Pratt put together a historic run of plate appearances.Pratt makes World Series history with record-breaking hitting streakSpanning across Games 4 and 5, Pratt set an all-time World Series rookie record by collecting six consecutive hits in six straight at-bats. He began the tear in Game 4 with a double, followed by two singles and his dramatic 12th-inning blast. He then picked up right where he left off the following night in Game 5, roping an RBI single off Drew Rasmussen in the second inning to tie Brian Doyle's 1978 rookie record of five straight hits. In the fifth inning, he cemented his place in baseball history with a single off reliever Kevin Kelly to reach six straight. Not only did he shatter the 48-year-old rookie milestone, but he also became the first player of any experience level to record six straight hits in the Fall Classic since David Ortiz did so for the Boston Red Sox in 2013. The streak showcased his elite visual coverage at the plate, as the six hits came against six different Rays pitchers using five entirely different pitch types.Pratt added another important contribution later in Game 5 with a sacrifice fly in the sixth inning that made it 4-0, falling just one shy of Billy Hatcher’s all-time overall record of seven consecutive safe appearances. The hit also extended a remarkable run of production: according to OptaSTATS, he became the first rookie in World Series history to record multiple RBIs in three consecutive games. For a player making his first major-league season, it was an extraordinary achievement on a stage where even established stars can struggle to produce consistently.Pratt finished the World Series with eight hits across the five games, while team-mate Jackson Chourio recorded 10. Chourio had the higher hit total, but the importance of Pratt's contributions made a compelling case for the shortstop as one of Milwaukee's most influential players during the championship run. His go-ahead hit in Game 2, his home run in Game 4 and his contribution to the remarkable fifth-inning sequence in Game 3 were among the moments that shaped the series.At 22 years and 71 days old, Pratt became the second-youngest player to record at least eight hits and seven RBIs in a World Series, according to Just Baseball. The two players ahead of him in that historical comparison were Juan Soto and Hank Aaron, placing the Brewers rookie in notable company. What made the achievement more striking was the number of games required: Pratt reached those figures in five games, while Soto and Aaron each took seven.The Brewers had taken a considerable financial risk in April, committing $50.75 million to a player who had yet to make his major-league debut. By October, Pratt was delivering important hits in a World Series, helping Milwaukee secure the first championship in franchise history. The organisation had backed his potential before the wider baseball world had seen him at the highest level, and his rookie season gave that decision an immediate and emphatic return.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: New MLB Trade Rumors Update Ronald Acuna Jr. Buzz After Braves Contract Option Exercised
articles.summary: Don't expect Ronald Acuña Jr. to be traded this winter.
articles.body:
Don't expect Ronald Acuña Jr. to be traded this winter.

According to Jon Morosi of MLB Network, such a deal is "seen as highly unlikely" despite Acuña entering the final year of his contract (the Atlanta Braves do hold a team option for 2028).

It shouldn't come as much of a surprise that the Braves don't want to trade a former NL MVP, five-time All-Star and three-time Silver Slugger who is only 28 years old and still very much in his prime years.

Knee and hamstring injuries have limited Acuña to just 251 games over the past three seasons and he had a down year in 2026 by his own lofty standards, hitting .255 with 20 homers, 55 RBI, 61 runs, 21 stolen bases and a .796 OPS across 107 games. His down year is a career year for most.

But there's little doubt that Acuña at full strength is an absolute superstar. His 162-game averages during his career are impressive: 36 homers, 90 RBI, 126 runs, 31 doubles, 40 stolen bases, 5.4 WAR and a .895 OPS.

Even if he never replicates the absurd numbers he put up in his 2023 MVP season (41 homers, 73 stolen bases, 1.012 OPS, 8.4 WAR), he's still an important piece of Atlanta's core and one of the more dynamic outfielders in the sport. Coming to terms on an extension would be far more favorable than losing him in a trade, especially after the Braves just won the NL East and reached the playoffs.

He's also currently one of the best bargains in the sport, with his team options in 2027 and 2028 only setting the team back a combined total of $34 million. On the open market, he'd probably earn around $34 million per season, so the Braves don't have much incentive to trade away a superstar on such an affordable contract, even considering his recent medical history.

Add it all up, and Monday's report shouldn't come as much of a surprise.

articles.title: Tigers INF Kevin McGonigle wins AL Rookie of the Year Award in landslide vote
articles.summary: McGonigle lived up to his billing and more in his rookie season, and now he's walking away with the American League Rookie of the Year Award.
articles.body:
Big things were expected of Detroit Tigers prospect Kevin McGonigle heading into the 2026 MLB season. The rookie ranked as the No. 2 overall prospect on most every reputable top-100 list entering the season, a spot reserved for a future perennial All-Star.

McGonigle lived up to that billing and more in his debut season, and now he's walking away with the American League Rookie of the Year Award.

MLB announced McGonigle as the winner on Monday. He received 28 of 30 first-place votes . McGonigle beat Cleveland Guardians pitcher Parker Messick and Boston Red Sox starter Payton Tolle for the award. Messick received the other two first-place votes .

Breaking down the numbers, it's tough to overstate the impact McGonigle had on the 2026 Tigers. The 22-year-old immediately justified the team's decision to stick him on the Opening Day roster, as he notched four hits in his first game. That proved to be a harbinger of what was to come for McGonigle, who posted a .278/.376/.430 slash line with 18 home runs during his rookie year.

In addition to his excellence at the plate, McGonigle received rave reviews for his strong defense at shortstop and third base. Because of that, he led the American League in bWAR — Baseball-Reference's version of WAR. Although McGonigle did not finish as a finalist for the MVP Award, that stat would indicate that he was also deserving of that honor.

McGonigle will happily settle for the Rookie of the Year Award. While both Messick and Tolle deserve recognition for their numbers, it was McGonigle and his all-around game that swayed most voters.

After a phenomenal rookie season, the sky is the limit for McGonigle. If the young superstar can build on his excellence as a rookie, an MVP season could be on the horizon before long.

articles.title: Kevin McGonigle, Sal Stewart Win AL, NL Rookie of the Year 2026 Awards, Full MLB Voting Results
articles.summary: Sal Stewart of the Cincinnati Reds and Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers were the best rookies in Major League Baseball this past season.
articles.body:
Sal Stewart of the Cincinnati Reds and Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers were the best rookies in Major League Baseball this past season.

Stewart took home the 2026 National League Rookie of the Year on Monday, while McGonigle captured the 2026 American League Rookie of the Year.

The finalists for the awards were announced earlier this month, and Carson Benge of the New York Mets and JJ Wetherholt of the St. Louis Cardinals joined Stewart in the National League race.

As for the American League, Parker Messick of the Cleveland Guardians and Payton Tolle of the Boston Red Sox were finalists alongside McGonigle.

The American League race was a bit like comparing apples to oranges, as McGonigle is an infielder while the other two finalists are pitchers. The two pitchers can be directly compared from a statistical perspective, but figuring out how those numbers stack up against McGonigle's offensive ones was a job for the voters.

McGonigle was an All-Star in his first season while slashing .278/.376/.430 with 18 home runs, 72 RBI and 12 stolen bases. He also appeared in 156 games for the Tigers as a durable and reliable staple in their lineup.

What's more, he led the American League with a wins above replacement (WAR) total of 7.1, per Baseball Reference .

Messick was also an All-Star with a sparkling 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186.1 innings for Cleveland, while Tolle finished with a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148.2 innings for Boston.

The National League race did not feature any pitchers, although there was perhaps more drama regarding the final result since it was something of a race between traditional power stats for Stewart and more advanced ones bolstering the cases for Benge and Wetherholt.

Stewart appeared in all 162 games and finished with a .263/.330/.457 slash line, 32 home runs, 112 RBI and 15 stolen bases. By crossing the 30-homer and 100-RBI barriers, he demonstrated just how impactful his bat was in the middle of the Reds' lineup.

However, his WAR of 2.0 was well behind Benge's mark of 4.3 and Wetherholt's total of 4.5.

Benge slashed .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 65 RBI and 22 stolen bases while also showing off an impressive throwing arm in the outfield that made him dangerous to run against during the season. As for Wetherholt, he was a dazzling defender and finished second to only Pete Crow-Armstrong in outs above average this season, per Baseball Savant .

Wetherholt was arguably the best defensive infielder in the league but still slashed .242/.339/.365 with 17 home runs, 51 RBI and 14 stolen bases.

It was a fascinating race with different cases to be made for each contender, but ultimately it was Stewart who took home the award.

articles.title: Sal Stewart wins 2026 NL Rookie of the Year Award after finishing third in MLB in RBI
articles.summary: Stewart is the ninth Reds player to win the award.
articles.body:
Cincinnati Reds first baseman Sal Stewart has been named the 2026 NL Rookie of the Year, capping off a strong debut season for the slugger.

Stewart joins Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle, who won the AL honor , as the rookie award winners.

Stewart finished with 20 of 30 first-place votes, and a total of 170 points, to outpace the other finalists for the award, New York Mets outfielder Carson Benge and St. Louis Cardinals second baseman JJ Wetherholt.

Stewart played in every game for the Reds this season. He slashed .263/.330/.457 while hitting 32 home runs and recording 112 RBI (third in MLB) across the 162 contests.

Cincinnati's first baseman debuted on Sept. 1, 2025. He played 18 games last year, which did not meet the threshold to end his rookie eligibility.

Stewart began the 2026 campaign as the Reds' starting first baseman. Cincinnati had struggled to fill the position since Joey Votto's last season with the team in 2023.

Cincy started the 2024 and '25 seasons with Christian Encarnacion-Strand at first base. This year, he started the year in the minors and was then traded to the Baltimore Orioles after Stewart cemented himself as the Reds' starter.

Stewart is the ninth player in Cincinnati history to win the NL Rookie of the Year Award. He joins Frank Robinson (1956), Pete Rose (1963), Tommy Helms (1966), Johnny Bench (1968), Pat Zachry (1976), Chris Sabo (1988), Scott Williamson (1999) and Jonathan India (2021).

Stewart, Wetherholt and Benge were the three finalists for the 2026 NL honor, in a race that proved more competitive than the AL version .

Wetherholt played in 139 games this season. While Stewart led him in most statistical categories, the Cardinals' second baseman had the edge in WAR. Stewart posted 2.0 bWAR as a first baseman while Wetherholt logged 4.5 bWAR at second.

Benge had 168 hits this season, seventh in MLB. The Mets outfielder's .282 average was 15th among qualified hitters. He posted 4.3 bWAR.

articles.title: Reds' Sal Stewart 'just getting started' with NL Rookie of Year award
articles.summary: Sal Stewart says he's "just getting started" after winning NL Rookie of the Year. He's the ninth player in Reds history to accomplish the feat.
articles.body:
LAS VEGAS — Sal Stewart had no sooner accepted the National League Rookie of the Year award than he embarked on the task of getting the Cincinnati Reds back to the playoffs next year.

Well, he planned to embark on that once the party in Miami with dozens of friends and family concludes at some point this week.

"Just a kid from Miami living his dream!" he said at the end of a video conference with Cincinnati media after becoming the ninth player in franchise history to win the award.

"You might wake up at 8. a.m., and I'm still gonna be out partying. I'll be enjoying it."

No matter how long that party might last, no matter how long a labor lockout might last once MLB's labor agreement expires Dec. 1, Stewart has already fixed his sights firmly on 2027 and helping lead the Reds from last place back to the postseason he experienced a month into his big-league career in 2025.

Reds Rookie of the Year winners | From Frank Robinson to Jonathan India

"My career is just getting started. I promise you that," he said. "I promise you this is just a steppingstone, and there's more to come.

"This season didn't go the way we wanted," he added, "but I feel like if I want to be the player that I want to be for this organization, (this award) is a good steppingstone to show everybody (coming up), 'Hey, I'm willing to do it. Everyone that comes up here better be willing to do it, to put your life on the line for your team.'

"I feel that will go a long way, and I feel our season will turn out better next year."

Sal Stewart's 2026 season | Looking back at outstanding Reds rookie

Stewart, 22, hit 32 home runs and drove in 112 runs in 2026, earning an All-Star selection and the Reds' first Rookie of the Year award since Jonathan India in 2021 – winning 20 of 30 first-place votes and beating second-place Carson Benge (seven first-place votes) of the Mets 170 points to 107. JJ Wetherholt (three) of the Cardinals was third with 99 points.

The award was a goal Stewart set for himself long before getting to spring training, even with a loaded field of impact rookies who figured to be in play across the league.

"Because so many people doubted me. So many people didn't think I could," he said. "I love that. My whole life I've been doubted. Even when I got drafted, I had people on MLB Network saying I was a bad decision. 'He didn't have a hit ability.' 'His power needed to come.' 'His defense was bad.'

"I don't forget those things," he said. "I keep all the receipts for all the people that talk. I just wanted to prove those people wrong."

The ultra competitive Stewart played all season with a level of confidence and apparent chip on his shoulder that belied his age and experience level. It especially showed up in high-leverage moments, with men in scoring position and in close-and-late game situations.

It's what led to RBI totals that led the league much of the season before Stewart eventually finished four behind the MLB leader.

Beyond the significance of being one of just seven players to play all 162 games this season, he preaches the value of an RBI stat that has fallen out of favor in this era of advanced stats and analytics – an appreciation instilled by his baseball mentors growing up and that boils down to situational hitting to try to win games.

"Whether it's a ground ball to shortstop with the infield back or whether it's a sac fly," he said. "You can't win a game if you don't drive in runs at the end of the day."

The Reds didn't have enough runs or enough wins regardless in this case. Which already seems to be Stewart's focus with the prestigious award in his back pocket.

He says he wants to get with team officials to find out what their plan is for him positionally next year – back to his original third base or staying primarily at first – then working this winter on getting better there.

And performing again, and helping lead others, to get back to the playoffs.

"I really want to win for this city," he said. "This award's great, but at the end of the day I don't like sitting down and watching the playoffs. I want to be playing in them. And that's something I've got to figure out a way to help my team do that.

"I know what we're capable of," he added. "We have the right guy at the helm (in manager Terry Francona). Tito knows what the expectation is. And he's the first one to make sure I'm living up to it, and if I'm not he's the first one calling me into his office making sure I'm living up to it. We know what it takes. We know what the expectation is. Losing's not fun, man. We do this to win."

Stewart is the fifth player in franchise history to earn All-Star selection and the Rookie of the Year award in the same season. The Reds' eight other Rookie of the Year winners (*-indicates All-Star):

"My career is just getting started. I promise you that," he said. "I promise you this is just a steppingstone, and there's more to come.

"This season didn't go the way we wanted," he added, "but I feel like if I want to be the player that I want to be for this organization, (this award) is a good steppingstone to show everybody (coming up), 'Hey, I'm willing to do it. Everyone that comes up here better be willing to do it, to put your life on the line for your team.'

"I feel that will go a long way, and I feel our season will turn out better next year."

Sal Stewart's 2026 season | Looking back at outstanding Reds rookie

Stewart, 22, hit 32 home runs and drove in 112 runs in 2026, earning an All-Star selection and the Reds' first Rookie of the Year award since Jonathan India in 2021 – winning 20 of 30 first-place votes and beating second-place Carson Benge (seven first-place votes) of the Mets 170 points to 107. JJ Wetherholt (three) of the Cardinals was third with 99 points.

The award was a goal Stewart set for himself long before getting to spring training, even with a loaded field of impact rookies who figured to be in play across the league.

"Because so many people doubted me. So many people didn't think I could," he said. "I love that. My whole life I've been doubted. Even when I got drafted, I had people on MLB Network saying I was a bad decision. 'He didn't have a hit ability.' 'His power needed to come.' 'His defense was bad.'

"I don't forget those things," he said. "I keep all the receipts for all the people that talk. I just wanted to prove those people wrong."

The ultra competitive Stewart played all season with a level of confidence and apparent chip on his shoulder that belied his age and experience level. It especially showed up in high-leverage moments, with men in scoring position and in close-and-late game situations.

It's what led to RBI totals that led the league much of the season before Stewart eventually finished four behind the MLB leader.

Beyond the significance of being one of just seven players to play all 162 games this season, he preaches the value of an RBI stat that has fallen out of favor in this era of advanced stats and analytics – an appreciation instilled by his baseball mentors growing up and that boils down to situational hitting to try to win games.

"Whether it's a ground ball to shortstop with the infield back or whether it's a sac fly," he said. "You can't win a game if you don't drive in runs at the end of the day."

The Reds didn't have enough runs or enough wins regardless in this case. Which already seems to be Stewart's focus with the prestigious award in his back pocket.

He says he wants to get with team officials to find out what their plan is for him positionally next year – back to his original third base or staying primarily at first – then working this winter on getting better there.

And performing again, and helping lead others, to get back to the playoffs.

"I really want to win for this city," he said. "This award's great, but at the end of the day I don't like sitting down and watching the playoffs. I want to be playing in them. And that's something I've got to figure out a way to help my team do that.

"I know what we're capable of," he added. "We have the right guy at the helm (in manager Terry Francona). Tito knows what the expectation is. And he's the first one to make sure I'm living up to it, and if I'm not he's the first one calling me into his office making sure I'm living up to it. We know what it takes. We know what the expectation is. Losing's not fun, man. We do this to win."
